headline: High risk of shared-repo prompt injection and write conflicts; Goose’s MCP extensibility raises the blast radius.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes git-tracked files and shares state via a shared git repo, while Goose reads/writes the user filesystem and can use MCP extensions. That creates a plausible content-to-instructions bridge through files, though no direct clipboard or message queue is documented. The pathway exists in default coding workflows, but it is not as direct as raw web-content parsing.
conditions: IF either agent consumes repository files as instructions rather than data, injected text can steer tool use.
IF Goose is configured with an MCP extension that reads Aider-authored files, file-based prompt injection becomes reachable.
mitigations: Keep instruction-like text out of shared repo files.
Add a short repo-level prompt-injection warning in CONTRIBUTING.md.
Use separate working directories for the two agents.
Review any MCP extension inputs before enabling them.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for agent-authored file content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch source code, and Aider explicitly handles model provider API keys via env vars while Goose handles model provider keys and extension-specific tokens. Because both can read/write the same code workspace and both may send file contents to configured model providers, sensitive code or secrets can flow between them through the shared workspace in default coding setups.
conditions: IF the two agents operate on the same repository checkout, file contents can be exposed across sessions.
IF either agent is pointed at files containing secrets, those contents may be transmitted to its configured model provider.
mitigations: Remove secrets from the shared repo before running either agent.
Use separate clones or worktrees per agent.
Restrict both agents to non-sensitive subdirectories.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately.
requires-engineering: enforce secret scanning before model calls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can modify git state and writes via git commits, and Goose can also modify git state and write the filesystem. Aider’s shared state is via a shared git repo, while Goose shares state via the filesystem. With overlapping write access and no locking described, concurrent edits can overwrite each other or corrupt repo state in default use.
conditions: IF both agents edit the same branch or worktree concurrently, git conflicts can occur.
IF Goose writes files that Aider later commits, one agent can silently overwrite the other’s changes.
mitigations: Run only one agent per branch at a time.
Use separate branches for Aider and Goose.
Commit or stash before switching agents.
Disable concurrent sessions on the same checkout.
requires-engineering: add file-level locking or merge arbitration.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider’s output is likely to be consumed as code edits or commit messages, and Goose can act on filesystem and MCP inputs. That makes Aider’s suggestions a plausible upstream input to Goose without a verification step. The pair is not documented as having a formal handoff protocol, so mistaken assumptions can cascade into incorrect edits or actions.
conditions: IF Goose is fed Aider-generated patches or summaries without review, errors can propagate.
IF either agent is allowed to act on the other’s output automatically, downstream mistakes become more likely.
mitigations: Require human review between agents.
Pass only diffs, not free-form instructions.
Ask Goose to restate assumptions before acting.
Limit Goose to read-only verification on Aider output.
requires-engineering: add structured handoff schemas with validation.

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source coding agents with no explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch documented. Aider handles model provider API keys and Goose handles extension-specific tokens, but the profiles do not show a compliance conflict by themselves. The other agent is not separately cited because no cross-border or policy mismatch is evidenced.
conditions: IF either agent is configured to process regulated data under a stricter policy than the other, a compliance gap may emerge.
IF Goose extensions send data to a non-approved service, policy review is required.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in the shared workspace.
Document approved data classes for both agents.
Review extension destinations before enabling them.
Keep retention settings aligned across tools.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data-class routing.
